How to actually use this

More problems is not the thing that improves you. These four are, and they are what strong competitors point at when asked.

1 · Ladder, do not wander

Work at your current rating and +100. When roughly 8 in 10 land inside 35 minutes, step up one rung. Jumping ahead feels productive and teaches nothing.

2 · Time-box at 35 minutes

Then read the editorial. Staring for three hours is the single biggest waste in competitive programming — the learning is in reading the solution after real struggle.

3 · Upsolve every contest

Do a virtual contest, then solve everything you could not finish during it. This is the habit most often named as the thing that actually moved someone’s rating.

4 · Re-solve failures after a week

A problem you needed the editorial for is not learned. Re-solve it cold seven days later. This is pattern recall under time pressure, and it decays.

One caveat, stated plainly: this is competitive programming, not Software Engineer interview prep. It will sharpen your implementation speed, binary search and graph instincts. It will also spend a lot of your time on constructive algorithms, number theory and game theory that interviews never ask about. Use it knowingly alongside the DSA track, not instead of it.

Any problem where a candidate answer can be checked faster than it can be found. If can(x) is monotone — true for everything above some threshold and false below — you can binary search the threshold in log time.

The giveaway phrase is minimise the maximum or maximise the minimum. That is binary search on the answer, essentially always.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Binary search on the answer — Guess a value, write a greedy or linear check(x), and halve the range. Most 1400–1900 problems tagged this are exactly this.
  • 02Monotone predicate — Prove check is monotone before you search. If it is not, binary search is silently wrong.
  • 03lower_bound / upper_bound — Search a sorted array or a prefix-sum array; often the second half of a two-pointer or sorting problem.
  • 04Binary search on a real interval — Fixed iteration count (about 100 rounds) instead of an epsilon comparison — safer and simpler.
  • 05Parallel binary search — Many queries, each needing its own threshold; process all of them level by level.

An integer used as a set. Feasible while n is at most about 20–24, because you enumerate all 2n subsets. The moment you see n ≤ 20 in the constraints, think bitmask.

n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit and n & -n isolates it. Those two show up in more solutions than any other bit trick.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Subset DP — dp[mask] over which elements are used — travelling salesman, assignment, covering. O(2n·n) is the standard shape.
  • 02Enumerate submasks — for (s = m; s; s = (s-1) & m) walks every submask of m. Total over all masks is 3n, not 4n.
  • 03Per-bit independence — Solve each of the 30 bit positions separately and combine. Very common in XOR problems.
  • 04XOR prefix — xor[i..j] = pre[j] ^ pre[i-1] — the XOR analogue of prefix sums.
  • 05Meet in the middle — Split n into two halves of n/2, enumerate both, and join. Turns 240 into 220.

Not a failure mode — a deliberate reading of the constraints. If n is 100 and the limit is 2 seconds, an O(n3) triple loop is the intended solution and anything cleverer is wasted effort.

Always compute the worst case before dismissing brute force. 108 simple operations runs in about a second; people abandon a correct O(n²) at n = 5000 for no reason.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Read the constraints first — n ≤ 20 → exponential. n ≤ 500 → O(n³). n ≤ 5000 → O(n²). n ≤ 105 → O(n log n).
  • 02Fix one variable, solve the rest — Loop over one element or one boundary and reduce to an easier subproblem. The single most common shape here.
  • 03Enumerate the answer's structure — Try every starting point, every pair, every split — when the count is small enough to allow it.
  • 04Small-to-large search space — Enumerate divisors, not multiples; enumerate the shorter string; enumerate the smaller side.
  • 05Brute force as a checker — Write it anyway and stress-test your fast solution against it. This is how you find the bug you cannot see.

Counting without enumerating. Almost always modulo 109+7, which means precomputed factorials and modular inverses are the first thing you write.

Precompute factorials and inverse factorials to 2×105 once, at the top of the file. Half of these problems become a one-line formula after that.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01nCr with precomputed factorials — fact[], inv_fact[], and Fermat's little theorem for the inverse. The standard opening move.
  • 02Stars and bars — Distributing k identical items into n boxes: C(k+n-1, n-1). Recognising it saves the whole problem.
  • 03Inclusion-exclusion — Count everything, subtract the bad cases, add back the double-subtracted. Watch for the alternating sign.
  • 04Complementary counting — Counting at least one is usually harder than total minus none.
  • 05Linearity of expectation — Sum the per-element probability and ignore dependence entirely. Turns terrifying problems into one line.

You are asked to build a valid answer, not count or optimise one. There is usually a simple pattern, and the work is finding it rather than implementing it.

Solve n = 1, 2, 3, 4 by hand on paper before writing anything. The pattern is nearly always visible by n = 4, and nearly never visible from staring at the statement.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Small cases by hand — Brute force n ≤ 6, print the answers, and look for the shape. This is the actual technique.
  • 02Find the invariant — Parity, a sum, a colouring. It tells you which cases are impossible — and the impossible case is usually half the marks.
  • 03Induction / extend by one — Build the answer for n from the answer for n-1. Very common for grids and permutations.
  • 04Symmetry and pairing — Pair the largest with the smallest, or mirror the two halves. Absurdly common in these problems.
  • 05Answer -1 first — Work out exactly when it is impossible before constructing. Most wrong answers here are missing that check.

When the naive solution is right but too slow, and the fix is a structure that makes one operation logarithmic. Recognising which structure is most of the work.

If the problem is range query plus point update, it is a Fenwick tree, and a Fenwick tree is fifteen lines. Do not reach for a segment tree until you actually need range updates.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Fenwick / BIT — Prefix sums with point updates in O(log n). Shortest to write — make it your default.
  • 02Segment tree — Range query and range update; lazy propagation when updates cover ranges. The general hammer.
  • 03Ordered set (multiset / policy tree) — Insert, erase, and find the k-th or count less than x in log time.
  • 04Monotonic stack / deque — Next-greater, sliding-window maximum, largest rectangle. O(n) where a heap would be O(n log n).
  • 05Offline + sort the queries — Sort queries by right endpoint and sweep. Turns many hard online problems into easy offline ones.

Depth-first traversal on graphs and grids, plus everything you can compute on the way down and back up. The single most reusable technique on this list.

Write it iteratively with an explicit stack, or raise the recursion limit — a recursive DFS on 105 nodes will stack-overflow in some languages and it is a miserable bug to find.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Flood fill on a grid — Count components, measure areas, mark regions. The most common single application.
  • 02Enter/exit times (tin/tout) — Flattens a tree into an array so subtree queries become range queries.
  • 03Return a value from the recursion — Subtree size, depth, max path — compute on the way back up. This is tree DP in disguise.
  • 04Cycle detection with colours — White/grey/black to find a back edge in a directed graph.
  • 05Bridges and articulation points — low[] values from DFS. Standard once you have written it once.

Split the input, solve both halves, and do the work that crosses the split. That crossing step is where the whole problem lives.

Counting inversions with merge sort is the template for this entire tag. Learn it properly and half of these become recognisable.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Merge sort counting — Count pairs across the split while merging — inversions, and every variation on count pairs with property P.
  • 02Solve the cross-boundary case — Handle left, right, then anything spanning the midpoint. The classic maximum-subarray D&C shape.
  • 03D&C optimisation on DP — When the optimal split point is monotone, it takes O(n²) DP down to O(n log n).
  • 04Binary lifting — Doubling on trees for k-th ancestor and LCA in O(log n).
  • 05CDQ divide and conquer — Offline handling of updates before queries; the go-to for 3-D partial order problems.

Optimal substructure plus overlapping subproblems. The hard part is never the code — it is choosing what the state means, and doing that badly is why a DP feels impossible.

Write the state as an English sentence first: dp[i][j] is the best value using the first i items with j capacity left. If you cannot write that sentence, you do not have the state right yet.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Define the state in words — Then the transition usually writes itself. Skipping this step is the number one cause of getting stuck.
  • 02Knapsack family — 0/1, unbounded, bounded, subset-sum. Recognising which one you have decides the loop order.
  • 03DP on subsequences of two strings — LCS, edit distance, distinct subsequences — the dp[i][j] grid over two inputs.
  • 04Rolling array — Keep only the last row or two. Turns O(n·m) memory into O(m) and is often required to pass.
  • 05Digit DP / bitmask DP — Counting numbers with a property up to N; DP over subsets when n ≤ 20.
  • 06DP on trees — dp[v][state] combined from children during DFS. Extremely common at 1700+.

Union-Find. Use it when the question is only ever are these two in the same group and groups merge but never split.

Path compression plus union by size is five lines and effectively O(1). Writing it without both is the difference between passing and timing out.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Path compression + union by size — Both, always. Either one alone gives you O(log n) instead of near-constant.
  • 02Count components — Start at n, decrement on each successful union. Answers half the problems tagged this.
  • 03Kruskal's MST — Sort edges, union if they are not already connected. The canonical use.
  • 04Offline, process in reverse — Deletions are hard, additions are easy — so run the queries backwards and union instead.
  • 05DSU with extra data — Store size, sum, or parity per root. Parity DSU solves bipartite-check and a is opposite to b problems.

Turning a string of operators, numbers and brackets into a value or a tree. Rare in contests, but the technique is fixed and worth owning once.

One recursive-descent parser you have written and understood beats memorising the shunting-yard algorithm you half-remember.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Recursive descent — One function per precedence level: expr → term → factor. The clearest approach by far.
  • 02Two stacks — Values and operators; pop and apply when precedence drops. The iterative equivalent.
  • 03Shunting-yard — Infix to postfix, then evaluate the postfix in one pass.
  • 04Handle the bracket recursively — On ( recurse, on ) return. Also the pattern for decoding nested strings.
  • 05Unary minus and whitespace — Where nearly every wrong answer in this tag comes from. Handle them deliberately.

Max-flow and min-cut. The real skill is modelling — recognising that a problem about assignment, selection or scheduling is secretly a flow network.

Max-flow equals min-cut is the theorem that makes this tag useful. Most flow problems are actually asking for the cut.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Dinic's algorithm — The practical max-flow to have in your library. Fast enough for essentially every contest constraint.
  • 02Max-flow min-cut — Remove the cheapest set of things to disconnect A from B is a min-cut, not a search.
  • 03Bipartite matching as flow — Source to left, left to right, right to sink, all capacity 1.
  • 04Project selection / closure — Profits and prerequisites → min-cut. A recognisable and very common modelling pattern.
  • 05Min-cost max-flow — When each unit of flow has a price — assignment problems with costs.

Two players, both playing optimally. The answer is almost never a simulation — it is a win/lose classification of positions.

Compute the win/lose status for the first ten positions by hand. The pattern is usually periodic and usually obvious, and then the whole problem collapses to a parity check.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Win/lose states — A position is losing if every move leads to a winning position, winning if any move leads to a losing one.
  • 02Find the pattern on small n — Brute force the first 10–20 values and look for periodicity. Solves most problems tagged this.
  • 03Sprague-Grundy — Independent subgames: compute each Grundy number as the mex of its moves, then XOR them together.
  • 04Nim and mex — Nim is losing exactly when the XOR of all piles is zero. Know this cold.
  • 05Parity arguments — A huge share of easier game problems reduce to whether some count is odd or even.

Points, lines, polygons. The algorithms are standard; the failure is precision. Stay in integers as long as you possibly can.

Use the cross product for orientation, never a computed slope. Slopes divide, division introduces error, and vertical lines break outright.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Cross product for orientation — Sign of the cross product gives left / right / collinear. The single most useful primitive here.
  • 02Convex hull — Andrew's monotone chain — sort, then build the two hulls. The standard implementation.
  • 03Integer arithmetic only — Compare squared distances instead of distances; multiply instead of dividing.
  • 04Sweep line — Sort events by x, maintain an active set. Segment intersection, closest pair, rectangle union.
  • 05Shoelace formula — Polygon area from vertices; twice the area stays an integer, so you can avoid floats entirely.

Pairing up two sides so nobody is used twice. Bipartite matching covers nearly all of it in practice.

By König's theorem, in a bipartite graph the maximum matching equals the minimum vertex cover. That converts a lot of covering problems into matching problems.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Kuhn's algorithm — Augmenting paths for bipartite matching. Short, and fast enough for typical constraints.
  • 02Hopcroft-Karp — O(E√V) when Kuhn is too slow on a large graph.
  • 03König's theorem — Max matching = min vertex cover; and max independent set = n minus max matching.
  • 04Hall's condition — Tells you whether a perfect matching exists at all, without constructing it.
  • 05Model it as flow — Any matching is a unit-capacity flow. Reach for this when the constraints are unusual.

The umbrella tag. Most of the work is recognising that the problem is a graph — states as nodes, transitions as edges — when nothing in the statement says graph.

If the problem has states and moves between them, it is a shortest-path problem even when it looks like a puzzle about a keypad or a jug of water.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01BFS for unweighted shortest path — The default. Also multi-source BFS by seeding the queue with every start.
  • 02Model states as nodes — (position, keys held), (cell, remaining fuel). This modelling step is the whole difficulty at 1800+.
  • 03Topological sort — Kahn's algorithm on in-degrees; also detects cycles by failing to emit every node.
  • 040-1 BFS — Edges weighted 0 or 1 → a deque instead of a heap, O(V+E) instead of O(E log V).
  • 05Connected components / bipartite check — Two-colouring during BFS answers a surprising number of problems outright.

Take the locally best option and never reconsider. Fast to write, and wrong far more often than people expect — which is why the proof matters more than the code.

Before you code it, try to construct a counterexample for two minutes. If you cannot, you probably have a correct greedy; if you can, you have just saved yourself a wrong-answer verdict.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Sort first — By value, by ratio, by end time. The sort key is the algorithm in most greedy problems.
  • 02Exchange argument — Show that swapping any pair towards your order never makes things worse. This is the actual proof technique.
  • 03Earliest deadline / earliest finish — Interval scheduling: sort by end time. The canonical correct greedy.
  • 04Heap-based greedy — Always take the current best — and push back what you displaced. Task scheduling, merging costs.
  • 05Two ends — Pair largest with smallest after sorting. Extremely common and usually right.

Turning a string or a set into a number you can compare in O(1). Powerful, and probabilistic — you are accepting a very small chance of collision.

Use two independent moduli, or a random base chosen at runtime. Fixed, well-known bases get anti-hash tests written against them on Codeforces specifically.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Polynomial rolling hash — Prefix hashes let you compare any two substrings in O(1). The core tool.
  • 02Double hashing — Two moduli, compared as a pair. Makes an intentional collision effectively impossible.
  • 03Randomised base — Pick the base at runtime from the clock. Defends against hacks aimed at a known base.
  • 04Hash a set with XOR of randoms — Assign each value a random 64-bit number; a set's hash is the XOR. Order-independent comparison.
  • 05Custom hash for unordered_map — The default is attackable and gets hacked to O(n²). Add a random salt.

No clever idea — just do exactly what the statement says, carefully. These are lost to bugs and off-by-ones, not to missing insight.

Read the statement twice and write the steps as comments before any code. Time lost here is almost always time spent re-reading, not time spent thinking.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Translate the statement literally — Resist optimising. Write what it says, then check the constraints allow it.
  • 02Break it into small functions — One job each. Long single functions are where the bugs hide in this tag.
  • 03Handle the edge cases up front — n = 1, empty input, all elements equal, maximum values. Write them down before coding.
  • 04Use the right container — A deque, a map, a set — picking correctly removes most of the fiddly index work.
  • 05Watch overflow — Sums of 105 values up to 109 exceed 32 bits. Use 64-bit by default.

You query a hidden input and get answers back. Almost always a search with a strict query budget, and the budget tells you the intended complexity.

Flush after every single query or you will time out with correct logic. A budget of about 20 queries for n = 106 means binary search; about 2n means a linear scan.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Read the budget as a hint — log n queries → binary search. n queries → one pass. n log n → sorting or divide and conquer.
  • 02Binary search on the hidden value — The most common interactive problem by a wide margin.
  • 03Flush after every query — cout << endl, fflush, or flush=True. Forgetting this looks exactly like a wrong algorithm.
  • 04Maintain a candidate set — Ask questions that halve the possibilities; the classic twenty-questions structure.
  • 05Write a local judge — Simulate the interactor yourself so you can actually debug. Worth the five minutes.

Formula-and-insight problems. Rarely long code — the difficulty is entirely in the observation, and once you have it the implementation is three lines.

If the answer for small n looks like a known sequence, compute the first six terms and look at the differences. Most of this tag is pattern recognition.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Compute small cases, find the formula — Brute force n = 1..8, then look for the closed form. The workhorse technique.
  • 02Modular arithmetic — Everything mod 109+7; modular inverse via Fermat when you need to divide.
  • 03Parity and invariants — What stays constant under the allowed operation? That is usually the entire problem.
  • 04Pigeonhole — With n+1 items in n boxes, two share — often the reason an answer is bounded and small.
  • 05Sum formulas — Arithmetic and geometric series, and n(n+1)/2 appearing in a loop you can then remove.

Grids to simulate, or matrix exponentiation to jump a linear recurrence forward billions of steps in log time.

n up to 1018 with a linear recurrence means matrix exponentiation. That constraint is essentially a label on the problem.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Matrix exponentiation — Express the recurrence as a matrix, then binary-exponentiate it. O(k³ log n).
  • 02Grid simulation — Rotate, transpose, spiral. Transpose then reverse rows is a 90-degree rotation.
  • 03Prefix sums in 2-D — Submatrix sum in O(1) with inclusion-exclusion on four corners.
  • 04Gaussian elimination — Solving linear systems; also the XOR-basis version over GF(2).
  • 05Careful index handling — Most losses in this tag are row/column confusion, not algorithmic failure.

Split the input in half, enumerate both halves separately, and combine. Turns 240 into two lots of 220 plus a join.

The tell is n ≤ 40 — too big for 2n, too small for polynomial. That constraint means this technique almost every time.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Split, enumerate, join — Generate all subset sums of each half, sort one side, binary search from the other.
  • 02Sort one half and binary search — The standard combine step. O(2n/2 log).
  • 03Two pointers on both halves — When you want pairs summing to at most X, sorted halves plus two pointers beats binary search.
  • 04Hash map for exact matches — Store one half in a map keyed by value; look up the complement from the other.
  • 05Watch the memory — 220 longs is already 8MB. Store the minimum you need per entry.

Divisibility, primes, GCD, modular arithmetic. Heavy in formulas, light in code, and a fixed toolkit that covers most problems.

Trial division to √n is enough to factorise a single number up to 1012. Reach for a sieve only when you need many numbers factorised.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Sieve of Eratosthenes — Primes up to 106–107; store the smallest prime factor to factorise any number in O(log n).
  • 02GCD / LCM and Euclid — gcd(a,b), and the extended version for modular inverses and linear Diophantine equations.
  • 03Modular inverse — Fermat's little theorem when the modulus is prime; extended Euclid otherwise.
  • 04Enumerate divisors to √n — Both i and n/i in one loop. Appears constantly.
  • 05CRT and Euler's totient — Combining congruences, and counting coprimes — the two named results worth knowing.

Expected values and probabilities, almost always modulo a prime, so 1/3 means the modular inverse of 3 rather than a decimal.

Linearity of expectation applies whether or not events are independent. That single fact trivialises a startling number of hard-looking problems.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Linearity of expectation — E[sum] = sum of E[each], always. Compute one element's contribution and multiply.
  • 02Contribution technique — For each element or pair, the probability it contributes — then sum. The dominant pattern.
  • 03Probability DP — dp[state] holding an expected value; transitions weighted by probability.
  • 04Fractions under a modulus — Represent p/q as p · q-1 mod M. Never use floating point here.
  • 05Expected number of steps — Set up the linear equations; for a simple chain they often telescope into a closed form.

Cheapest route through a weighted graph. Which algorithm you need is decided entirely by the edge weights.

Dijkstra breaks on negative edges — not slowly, but silently and wrongly. Check the weights before you pick the algorithm.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Dijkstra with a heap — Non-negative weights. O(E log V). The default choice.
  • 020-1 BFS — Weights only 0 or 1 → a deque, giving O(V+E).
  • 03Bellman-Ford — Negative edges, and detects negative cycles. Also the right tool for at most k edges constraints.
  • 04Floyd-Warshall — All pairs, n ≤ 500. Three loops with k on the outside — the order matters.
  • 05Layered / state graphs — Node becomes (vertex, extra state) — fuel left, tickets used, parity of moves.

Sorting as the setup rather than the goal. Almost always sort by the right key, then the answer is one linear pass.

Choosing the comparator is the problem. Once the order is right, these usually collapse to a greedy scan.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Sort by a custom key — By ratio, by end time, by difference. The insight lives in the comparator.
  • 02Sort then two pointers — Sorted input makes pair-finding linear instead of quadratic.
  • 03Coordinate compression — Map large or sparse values onto 0..n-1 so you can index arrays by them.
  • 04Sort events (sweep line) — Starts and ends as separate events, sorted by position, with a running counter.
  • 05Counting sort — Values in a small range → O(n) instead of O(n log n).

Suffix arrays, suffix automata and Z/prefix functions. Heavy machinery for substring questions that a hash cannot answer.

Try hashing first — it solves most substring comparison problems in a fraction of the code. Reach for suffix structures when you need all distinct substrings or the longest repeat.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Z-function / prefix function — Linear-time pattern matching (KMP) and the longest border. Cheapest tool in the tag.
  • 02Suffix array + LCP — Sort all suffixes, then Kasai's algorithm for LCP. Distinct substrings, longest repeated substring.
  • 03Suffix automaton — Every distinct substring as a state; counts occurrences and distinct substrings in linear time.
  • 04Aho-Corasick — Many patterns matched against one text in a single pass — a trie plus failure links.
  • 05Hashing as the shortcut — Often replaces all of the above with twenty lines. Try it before committing.

Everything from simple character counting to pattern matching. The easy end is frequency arrays; the hard end is prefix functions and hashing.

A 26-length frequency array answers more string problems than any algorithm on this list. Try counting before you try anything clever.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Frequency counting — A 26-length array or a map. Anagrams, palindrome feasibility, character constraints.
  • 02Two pointers on a string — Palindrome checks, and the longest substring with a property.
  • 03Prefix function (KMP) — Pattern search, period detection, and the longest border, all in O(n).
  • 04Rolling hash — Compare any two substrings in O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.
  • 05Expand around centre — All palindromic substrings in O(n²) — short and usually fast enough.

For a function that rises then falls (or the reverse) with a single peak. Binary search finds a threshold; ternary search finds an extremum.

Prove the function is unimodal first. Ternary search on a function with two local maxima returns a confidently wrong answer.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Ternary search on reals — Fixed iteration count — about 200 rounds — rather than an epsilon test.
  • 02Ternary search on integers — Shrink until the range is about three wide, then check those by hand.
  • 03Prove unimodality — Convex or concave. Often a sum of convex functions, which is itself convex.
  • 04Nested ternary search — Two variables, one search inside the other. O(log²) and surprisingly common.
  • 05Combine with binary search — Ternary for the optimum, then binary search either side of it for a threshold.

A connected acyclic graph, which makes almost everything easier: exactly one path between any two nodes, and no cycles to guard against.

Root the tree at node 1 and run one DFS computing subtree values on the way back up. That single pattern solves a large share of this tag.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Root it and DFS — Compute subtree size, depth, and sums on the way back up. The default opening.
  • 02Tree DP — dp[v][state] merged from children — independent set, matching, colouring on trees.
  • 03LCA by binary lifting — O(log n) per query after O(n log n) preprocessing; gives path lengths for free.
  • 04Euler tour / flattening — Subtree becomes a contiguous range, so a Fenwick tree answers subtree queries.
  • 05Diameter by two BFS — Farthest node from anywhere, then farthest from that. Two passes, no DP needed.
  • 06Small-to-large merging — Merge child maps into the largest child's map. O(n log n) total for subtree counting.

Two indices moving in one direction over a sorted or sequential structure, so a quadratic scan becomes linear. Sliding window is the same idea with one pointer chasing the other.

The window is valid, so move right; the window is invalid, so move left. If you can state the shrink condition in one sentence, you have already solved it.

Techniques that solve most of these
  • 01Sliding window with a shrink condition — Grow right, shrink left while invalid. The dominant shape in this tag.
  • 02Converging pointers on sorted input — One at each end, moving inward — pair sums, container problems.
  • 03Fast and slow pointers — Cycle detection, and finding the middle in one pass.
  • 04Window counts in a map — Maintain frequencies incrementally instead of recomputing the window each step.
  • 05Sort, then two pointers — When the input is not already ordered, sorting first is what makes the technique apply.
